rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a sharp inference and a made-up premise. Its proof line, "do not assert the absence," is the grown-up move on the sales-team question. B has good bones, but "spent years refusing to enter" and "Selling to a second buyer without a sales team" smuggle in facts the update did not give. That is how a pitch dies in the first follow-up.
gaps_in_A: "who's threatened" is a clean conflict lens, but it still needs a real opponent; no incumbent tool, switching customer, or competitor response is in the facts.
"product managers want a tool that feels built for engineers" assumes PM demand before a PM, designer, or beta customer exists in the update.
It skips a possible customer/practitioner lens: no kept angle asks whether roadmaps living outside engineers' work creates a workflow cost PMs will describe on record.
gaps_in_B: "spent years refusing to enter" is invented history. The update says Linear is expanding beyond engineering teams, not that it previously refused the market.
"Jira/Asana/Notion competitive set" names competitors the update did not supply, then the refused section calls "Linear takes on Jira" a hallucination. Pick a lane.
"Selling to a second buyer without a sales team" asserts absence. The facts only say no enterprise sales team is mentioned.
"Stakeholder views are, by definition, for people who open the tool weekly, not hourly" and "roadmap in one tool, execution in another" decorate missing user-behavior proof as if it were known.
